l: the Jews, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 18
s: The officers of the Jews seize and bind Jesus and lead him to Annas. They bring him to the Praetorium but do not enter, to avoid defilement before the Passover, tell Pilate it is illegal for them to put anyone to death, and shout for Barabbas, a robber, instead of Jesus.

l: The Gospel According to John, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 19
s: Pilate has Jesus flogged, and the soldiers mock him with a crown of thorns and a purple garment. Pilate presents him to the chief priests and officers, who demand crucifixion, claiming he made himself the Son of God and pressing Pilate with the charge that he opposes Caesar. Pilate yields and delivers Jesus to be crucified at Golgotha between two others, with a title in Hebrew, Latin, and Greek reading "JESUS OF NAZARETH, THE KING OF THE JEWS." The soldiers divide his garments, Jesus entrusts his mother to the disciple he loved, says "It is finished," and dies; a soldier pierces his side. Joseph of Arimathaea and Nicodemus then bind his body with spices and lay it in a new tomb in a nearby garden.

l: Jesus, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 19
s: Jesus is flogged, mocked with a crown of thorns and purple garment, and brought out by Pilate. He tells Pilate that Pilate would have no power unless it were given from above, and that the one who delivered him has greater sin. He carries his cross to Golgotha and is crucified between two others. He entrusts his mother to the disciple he loved, says "I am thirsty," receives vinegar, says "It is finished," and gives up his spirit. His side is pierced after death, and his body is buried in a new tomb.

l: Pilate, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 19
s: Pilate flogs Jesus, brings him out, and repeatedly states he finds no basis for a charge. He becomes more afraid on hearing that Jesus claimed to be the Son of God, questions Jesus, and seeks to release him. Pressed by the charge that releasing him makes him no friend of Caesar, he sits on the judgment seat and delivers Jesus to be crucified. He writes the title for the cross and refuses to change it, saying "What I have written, I have written." He gives Joseph permission to take the body.

l: the Jews, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 19
s: The Jews answer Pilate that by their law Jesus ought to die because he made himself the Son of God. They cry out that releasing him would make Pilate no friend of Caesar. They ask Pilate to have the legs of the crucified broken so the bodies can be removed before the special Sabbath. Many of them read the title on the cross, and their Preparation Day leads to Jesus being laid in the nearby tomb.

l: chief priests, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 19
s: The chief priests and officers shout "Crucify! Crucify!" when they see Jesus. They declare "We have no king but Caesar!" They later ask Pilate to change the title to say Jesus claimed to be King of the Jews, and Pilate refuses.

l: soldiers, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 19
s: The soldiers twist a crown of thorns, dress Jesus in purple, mock him as "King of the Jews," and slap him. After crucifying him they divide his garments into four parts and cast lots for the seamless tunic. They break the legs of the two others but find Jesus already dead, so one of them pierces his side with a spear, and blood and water come out.

l: Golgotha, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 19
s: Golgotha, called "The Place of a Skull" and named in Hebrew, is where Jesus is taken carrying his cross and crucified. It is near the city, and a garden with a new tomb lies in that place.

l: cross (Jesus' cross), The Gospel According to John, Chapter 19
s: Jesus bears his cross to Golgotha. Pilate's title, "JESUS OF NAZARETH, THE KING OF THE JEWS," is placed on it, written in Hebrew, Latin, and Greek. The Jews wish the bodies not to remain on the crosses during the Sabbath.

l: crucifixion of Jesus, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 19
s: Jesus is crucified at Golgotha with two others, one on either side and Jesus in the middle. The soldiers divide his garments, and several women and the beloved disciple stand by. He is given vinegar, declares "It is finished," and dies. The others' legs are broken but his are not, and his side is pierced, which the text says fulfills Scripture.

l: Mary (Jesus' mother), The Gospel According to John, Chapter 19
s: Jesus' mother stands by the cross with her sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene. Jesus says to her, "Woman, behold, your son!" and from that hour the disciple takes her into his own home.

l: disciple whom Jesus loved, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 19
s: The disciple whom Jesus loved stands by the cross. Jesus tells him "Behold, your mother!" and from that hour he takes her to his own home. The text identifies him as one who has seen and testified, and whose testimony is true.

l: Joseph of Arimathaea, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 19
s: Joseph of Arimathaea, a disciple of Jesus secretly for fear of the Jews, asks Pilate for Jesus' body. Pilate gives permission, and Joseph takes the body away. With Nicodemus he binds it in linen cloths with spices and lays it in the tomb.

l: Nicodemus, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 19
s: Nicodemus, who first came to Jesus by night, brings about a hundred Roman pounds of myrrh and aloes. He helps take Jesus' body and bind it in linen cloths with the spices according to Jewish burial custom.

l: garden tomb, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 19
s: The tomb lies in a garden at the place where Jesus was crucified. It is new, and no one had ever been laid in it. Because it was near and it was the Jews' Preparation Day, Jesus is laid there.

l: burial of Jesus, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 19
s: After Pilate grants permission, Joseph of Arimathaea and Nicodemus take Jesus' body and bind it in linen cloths with spices, as is the Jewish burial custom. They lay it in the new tomb in the garden near the crucifixion site because of the Preparation Day.

l: The Gospel According to John, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 20
s: On the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene finds the stone removed from the tomb and tells Simon Peter and the other disciple whom Jesus loved, who run to the tomb, find the linen cloths, and the other disciple believes. Mary stays weeping, sees two angels, then meets Jesus, whom she at first takes for the gardener, and recognizes him when he calls her name. Jesus sends her to tell his brothers he is ascending to his Father, and she reports to the disciples. That evening Jesus appears to the disciples behind locked doors, shows his hands and side, sends them, and breathes the Holy Spirit on them. A week later he appears again for Thomas, who had doubted, and Thomas declares 'My Lord and my God!'; the chapter closes by stating the purpose of the written signs.

l: Jesus, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 20
s: Jesus appears to Mary Magdalene at the tomb, calls her by name, and tells her not to hold him since he has not yet ascended to his Father, sending her to his brothers. That evening he stands among the locked-in disciples, says 'Peace be to you,' shows his hands and side, sends them as the Father sent him, and breathes on them to give the Holy Spirit. After eight days he appears again and invites Thomas to touch his hands and side, and blesses those who believe without seeing.

l: Mary Magdalene, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 20
s: Mary Magdalene goes to the tomb while it is dark, finds the stone taken away, and runs to tell Simon Peter and the other disciple. She stays weeping at the tomb, sees two angels, and meets Jesus, thinking him the gardener until he says her name and she answers 'Rabboni!' She then tells the disciples that she has seen the Lord and what he said to her.

l: Simon Peter, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 20
s: Simon Peter hears Mary's report and runs with the other disciple to the tomb. He is outrun, but he is the first to enter and sees the linen cloths and the head cloth rolled up by itself. The disciples then go back to their homes.

l: disciple whom Jesus loved, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 20
s: The other disciple whom Jesus loved runs with Peter to the tomb and outruns him, arriving first, and stoops to look in without entering. He then enters after Peter, sees the cloths, and believes. It is noted that they did not yet know the Scripture that Jesus must rise from the dead.

l: Thomas, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 20
s: Thomas, one of the twelve, called Didymus, is absent when Jesus first appears to the disciples. He refuses to believe their report unless he sees the nail prints and puts his finger and hand into Jesus' hands and side. When Jesus appears eight days later and invites him to touch, Thomas answers 'My Lord and my God!'

l: disciples (Jesus's disciples), The Gospel According to John, Chapter 20
s: The disciples are assembled behind locked doors for fear of the Jews when Jesus comes, says 'Peace be to you,' and shows them his hands and side; they are glad. Jesus sends them as the Father sent him, breathes the Holy Spirit on them, and speaks of forgiving and retaining sins. They tell Thomas 'We have seen the Lord!' and are together with him when Jesus appears again after eight days.

l: tomb (Jesus' tomb), The Gospel According to John, Chapter 20
s: The tomb is found with its stone taken away, prompting Mary's report and the visit of Peter and the other disciple, who see the linen cloths and the separately rolled-up head cloth. Mary later looks in and sees two angels in white sitting where Jesus' body had lain, at the head and at the feet.

l: Jesus' resurrection, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 20
s: The resurrection is shown through the empty tomb, the angels, and Jesus' appearances to Mary Magdalene, to the disciples, and to Thomas. The text notes the disciples did not yet know the Scripture that he must rise from the dead. Jesus says he is ascending to his Father and God, and the chapter states that the signs are written so that readers may believe he is the Christ, the Son of God.

l: The Gospel According to John, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 21
s: Jesus reveals himself again to seven disciples at the sea of Tiberias, including Simon Peter, Thomas, Nathanael, and the sons of Zebedee. After a night of catching nothing, they follow Jesus' instruction from the beach to cast the net on the right side and haul in one hundred fifty-three fish without the net tearing. The disciple whom Jesus loved recognizes the Lord, Peter throws himself into the sea, and Jesus serves the disciples bread and fish for breakfast. Jesus then asks Peter three times whether he loves him, commissions him to feed his lambs and sheep, and signifies the kind of death by which Peter will glorify God, telling him to follow. When Peter asks about the beloved disciple, Jesus says it is no concern of Peter's, and the text clarifies that Jesus did not say that disciple wouldn't die; the chapter closes by identifying that disciple as the witness who wrote these things.

l: Jesus, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 21
s: Jesus stands on the beach at daybreak, unrecognized, and tells the disciples to cast the net on the right side, leading to a huge catch. He serves them bread and fish, asks Peter three times about his love, commissions him to feed his sheep, and tells him to follow. He also tells Peter that the beloved disciple's fate is none of his concern.

l: Simon Peter, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 21
s: Simon Peter proposes going fishing, and on hearing it is the Lord, wraps his coat around himself and throws himself into the sea. He later draws the net to land and is questioned three times by Jesus about his love, grieving at the third question, and is commissioned to feed Jesus' lambs and sheep. Jesus signifies that Peter will be carried where he doesn't want to go in a death that glorifies God, and tells him to follow.

l: disciple whom Jesus loved, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 21
s: This disciple is the first to recognize Jesus on the beach, saying to Peter, "It's the Lord!" He is seen following Jesus and Peter, and is identified as the one who leaned on Jesus' chest at the supper. A rumor that he would not die arises, which the text corrects, and he is identified as the one who testifies about and wrote these things.

l: disciples (Jesus's disciples), The Gospel According to John, Chapter 21
s: Seven disciples are together at the sea of Tiberias, go out fishing with Peter, and catch nothing all night. They do not recognize Jesus at first, then obey him, bring the loaded net to land in the little boat, and eat the breakfast he gives them, none daring to ask who he is.

l: net (the disciples' net), The Gospel According to John, Chapter 21
s: The net is cast on the right side of the boat at Jesus' word and becomes too full of fish to draw in. The disciples drag it to land, and Peter pulls it ashore holding one hundred fifty-three great fish, yet it is not torn.

l: fish (the great catch), The Gospel According to John, Chapter 21
s: The fish fill the net so completely that the disciples cannot haul it in, and number one hundred fifty-three great fish. Jesus asks for some of them to be brought, while he already has fish laid on a fire of coals.

l: breakfast (Jesus' meal on the beach), The Gospel According to John, Chapter 21
s: On landing, the disciples find a fire of coals with fish and bread laid on it. Jesus invites them to come and eat, takes the bread and gives it to them, and the fish likewise. None dares ask who he is, knowing it is the Lord, and the conversation with Peter follows after they have eaten.

l: fishing trip (night fishing), The Gospel According to John, Chapter 21
s: Peter announces he is going fishing, and the others say they will come too, so they enter the boat. They catch nothing that night, until Jesus' instruction at daybreak changes the outcome.

l: Jesus' appearance to the disciples, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 21
s: Jesus reveals himself at the sea of Tiberias, standing on the beach unrecognized until the large catch prompts recognition. The text counts this as the third time he was revealed to his disciples after rising from the dead.

l: Jesus' questioning of Peter's love, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 21
s: After breakfast Jesus asks Simon, son of Jonah, three times whether he loves him, the first time adding "more than these." Peter answers each time that Jesus knows he has affection for him, and is grieved at the third asking. Each answer is met with a charge: feed my lambs, tend my sheep, feed my sheep.

l: Peter's future death, The Gospel According to John, Chapter 21
s: Jesus tells Peter that though he dressed himself and walked where he wished when young, in old age he will stretch out his hands and another will dress and carry him where he doesn't want to go. The text explains this signifies the kind of death by which Peter would glorify God, after which Jesus says, "Follow me."

The opening chapter of John's First Letter has the authors declare what they have heard, seen, and touched concerning the Word of life, which was with the Father and was revealed to them. They write so that the readers may share fellowship with them and with the Father and his Son, Jesus Christ, and so that the authors' joy may be fulfilled. The message they announce is that God is light and in him is no darkness at all. The chapter then contrasts walking in darkness, which makes claims of fellowship a lie, with walking in the light, where the blood of Jesus Christ cleanses from all sin. It closes by saying that denying sin deceives us and makes God a liar, while confessing sins brings forgiveness and cleansing from the faithful and righteous God.

God is declared to be light, with no darkness at all in him, and this is the message the authors heard and announce. He is called faithful and righteous, forgiving and cleansing the sins of those who confess them. Claiming to have not sinned makes him a liar.
Jesus Christ is called the Son of the Father, and the authors' fellowship is with the Father and with him. His blood cleanses those who walk in the light from all sin.
The Word of life existed from the beginning and was heard, seen with eyes, and touched by the authors' hands. The life was revealed to them; it is the eternal life that was with the Father.

l: authors (the writers of the letter), 1 John, 1 John / Chapter 1
s: The authors testify to having heard, seen, and touched the Word of life, and they declare it to the readers. They write so that the readers may have fellowship with them and so that their own joy may be fulfilled. They include themselves in the statements about sin, saying 'we' when speaking of deception and confession.

l: children of God, 1 John, 1 John / Chapter 1
s: The readers are addressed by the authors, who declare what they have seen and heard so that the readers may share fellowship with them and with the Father and the Son. They are given the message that God is light and are shown the conditions of walking in light versus darkness.

Fellowship is the purpose of the authors' declaration: that the readers may share it with them, and that it is with the Father and his Son, Jesus Christ. Claiming fellowship with God while walking in darkness is a lie, whereas walking in the light brings fellowship with one another.
Light is what God is, and walking in it as he is in the light brings fellowship with one another and cleansing by the blood of Jesus Christ from all sin.

l: light and darkness, 1 John, 1 John / Chapter 1
s: There is no darkness at all in God. Those who say they have fellowship with him yet walk in darkness lie and do not tell the truth.

Saying we have no sin deceives ourselves, and saying we haven't sinned makes God a liar, with his word not in us. Sin is cleansed by the blood of Jesus Christ, and confessing sins results in God's forgiveness and cleansing from all unrighteousness.

In Chapter 2 the writer addresses his readers as little children, telling them he writes so they may not sin and that Jesus Christ, the righteous Counselor with the Father, is the atoning sacrifice for the sins of the whole world. Knowing him is shown by keeping his commandments and walking as he walked, and the old commandment, which is also new, is to love one's brother rather than hate him. The readers are told not to love the world, which is passing away with its lusts, while whoever does God's will remains forever. The writer warns that many antichrists have arisen, who went out from the community and deny that Jesus is the Christ, the Father and the Son. He urges the readers to let what they heard from the beginning and the anointing from the Holy One remain in them, so they remain in the Son and the Father and have boldness at his appearing.

Jesus Christ is called the righteous Counselor with the Father and the atoning sacrifice for the sins of the readers and of the whole world. Those who say they remain in him ought to walk just as he walked, and the readers are urged to remain in him so they may have boldness when he appears. Denying that Jesus is the Christ marks the Antichrist.

The Father has Jesus Christ as a Counselor with him, and the readers are said to know him. Whoever loves the world does not have the Father's love, and whoever denies the Son does not have the Father, while whoever confesses the Son has the Father also. The things of the world are not the Father's.

The readers are addressed as little children whose sins are forgiven for his name's sake and who know the Father. They have an anointing from the Holy One, have knowledge, and are told to avoid loving the world, to let what they heard from the beginning remain in them, and to remain in him. The writer says he wrote because they know the truth, and also concerning those who would lead them astray.

Many antichrists have arisen, which shows that it is the final hour. They went out from the community because they did not belong to it, and that departure revealed that none of them belong to it. The Antichrist is identified as the liar who denies that Jesus is the Christ and denies the Father and the Son.

The readers are told not to love the world or its things, for loving it means the Father's love is not in a person. All that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes and the pride of life, belongs to the world and not to the Father. The world is passing away with its lusts, while the one who does God's will remains forever.

Keeping his commandments is how we know that we know him, and the one who claims to know him without keeping them is a liar. The writer calls his commandment both old, the word heard from the beginning, and new, true in him and in the readers because the darkness is passing and the true light already shines. Whoever keeps his word has God's love perfected in him.

l: love and hate of brother, 1 John, Chapter 2
s: Whoever says he is in the light but hates his brother is still in darkness, walks in darkness, does not know where he is going, and has been blinded by the darkness. Whoever loves his brother remains in the light and has no occasion for stumbling in him.

Chapter 3 describes believers as children of God, loved by the Father, who will be like him when he is revealed and who purify themselves in hope. It contrasts those who do righteousness and remain in him with those who sin and are of the devil, noting that the Son of God was revealed to take away sins and destroy the devil's works. The chapter makes love for one another the message from the beginning, contrasting it with Cain, who killed his brother, and says the world hates believers. It defines love by the laying down of his life for us and calls for love in deed and truth, including help for a brother in need. It closes with confidence toward God, who is greater than our hearts, and the commandment to believe in the name of his Son, Jesus Christ, and love one another, with the Spirit as the sign that he remains in us.

God the Father has given great love so that believers are called his children. He is greater than the heart and knows all things, gives what is asked of him by those who keep his commandments, and gave the Spirit as the sign that he remains in us.

Jesus Christ, called the Son of God, was revealed to take away sins and to destroy the works of the devil, and no sin is in him. He laid down his life for us, and believing in his name is part of God's commandment.

Believers are now children of God, though what they will be is not yet revealed; when he is revealed they will be like him, seeing him as he is. They are recognized by doing righteousness and loving their brothers, they are born of God and do not commit sin, and the world does not know them.

The devil has been sinning from the beginning, and whoever sins is of the devil. The Son of God was revealed to destroy his works, and those who do not do righteousness or love their brother are marked as his children.
Sin is described as lawlessness, and whoever sins has not seen or known him. Those born of God do not commit sin because his seed remains in them, and the Son of God was revealed to take sins away.

Love for one another is the message heard from the beginning and a sign of having passed from death into life, while hating a brother is likened to murder, as in Cain's killing of his brother. Love is known through Christ laying down his life, and it must be shown in deed and truth, including by sharing the world's goods with a brother in need.

The author addresses beloved readers, urging them to test spirits because many false prophets have gone into the world, and giving confession that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh as the test of what is of God. He says the readers have overcome the false teachers because the one in them is greater than the one in the world. He then calls them to love one another, since God is love and God showed his love by sending his only born Son as the atoning sacrifice for sins. The author teaches that remaining in love means remaining in God, that perfect love casts out fear, and that anyone who claims to love God but hates his brother is a liar. The chapter ends with the commandment that he who loves God should also love his brother.

God is described as love itself, and as the one who first loved believers and sent his only born Son into the world so that they might live through him. No one has seen God, but he remains in those who love one another and confess Jesus as his Son, and he has given them of his Spirit.

Confessing that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is given as the test of whether a spirit is of God. He is the only born Son whom the Father sent into the world as the atoning sacrifice for sins and as the Savior of the world, and whoever confesses him as the Son of God has God remaining in them.

Many false prophets have gone out into the world, and their spirit is identified with the spirit of the Antichrist, which is already in the world. They do not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh, they are of the world and speak of the world, and the world hears them.

Love is of God, and everyone who loves has been born of God and knows God, while he who does not love does not know God. God's love was shown in sending his Son, perfect love casts out fear, and love for God must show itself in love for one's brother, which is a commandment from him.

The readers are told to test the spirits, and are assured that they are of God and have overcome the false prophets because greater is he who is in them than he who is in the world. They are urged to love one another, and the author says that he who knows God listens to the authors, and that believers remain in God and he in them through his Spirit, with boldness for the day of judgment.

Chapter 5 teaches that whoever believes Jesus is the Christ has been born of God, and that loving God means keeping his commandments, which are not grievous. Faith in Jesus as the Son of God is the victory that overcomes the world. Jesus Christ came by water and blood, and the Spirit, the water, and the blood agree as one in testifying about him. God's testimony is that he gave eternal life, which is in his Son, so those who have the Son have life. The writer closes by discussing confident prayer according to God's will, sin leading and not leading to death, the one born of God who keeps himself from the evil one, and a warning to little children to keep themselves from idols.

Jesus Christ is declared to be the Son of God, and whoever believes he is the Christ has been born of God. He came by water and blood, not by water only, and God's testimony concerning him is that eternal life is in him. He is called the true God and eternal life, and believers are in him.

God is the Father who has given testimony concerning his Son, which is greater than the witness of men. He gave eternal life to us in his Son, and he listens to those who ask according to his will. Anyone who does not believe his testimony makes him a liar.

The children of God are known by loving God and keeping his commandments. Whoever loves the Father also loves the child born of him. Whoever is born of God doesn't sin but keeps himself, and the evil one doesn't touch him.
Loving God is defined as keeping his commandments, and keeping them is how we know we love God's children. The commandments are said to be not grievous.
Faith is named as the victory that has overcome the world. Whatever is born of God overcomes the world, and the one who overcomes is he who believes that Jesus is the Son of God.

Three testify: the Spirit, the water, and the blood, and the three agree as one. The Spirit testifies because the Spirit is the truth. God's testimony is that he gave eternal life in his Son, and the one who believes has this testimony in himself.
Eternal life is what God gave to us, and it is in his Son. He who has the Son has the life, and he who doesn't have the Son doesn't. The writer says he wrote so believers may know they have it.

All unrighteousness is sin, and there is sin not leading to death and sin leading to death. For a brother's sin not leading to death, one should ask and God will give life. About sin leading to death, the writer does not say to make a request.

Believers are those who believe in the name of the Son of God, and they are told they may know they have eternal life and continue to believe. They have boldness toward God that he hears requests made according to his will. They know they are of God while the whole world lies in the power of the evil one, and they are urged to keep themselves from idols.

In 2 John 1, the elder writes to the chosen lady and her children, whom he loves in truth along with all who know the truth. He wishes them grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Jesus Christ, and rejoices that some of her children walk in truth. He urges them to love one another and to walk according to the commandment they have had from the beginning. He warns that many deceivers, who deny that Jesus Christ came in the flesh, have gone out into the world, and that those who do not remain in the teaching of Christ do not have God. He tells her not to welcome anyone who does not bring this teaching, and says he hopes to visit face to face, closing with greetings from the children of her chosen sister.

The elder writes to the chosen lady and her children, whom he loves in truth. He rejoices that some of her children walk in truth, begs her to love one another, warns against deceivers, and hopes to visit and speak face to face so their joy may be full.

l: chosen lady (the elder's addressee), 2 John, 2 John / Chapter 1
s: The chosen lady is addressed by the elder as the recipient of the letter and is begged to love one another. She is instructed not to receive into her house or welcome anyone who does not bring the teaching, since welcoming such a person means sharing in his evil deeds.

l: children (the chosen lady's children), 2 John, 2 John / Chapter 1
s: The chosen lady's children are loved by the elder in truth, and he rejoices that he has found some of them walking in truth as commanded by the Father. The children of her chosen sister send greetings at the end of the letter.

l: God the Father, 2 John, 2 John / Chapter 1
s: God the Father is named as a source of grace, mercy, and peace, together with Jesus Christ, the Son of the Father. He is the one who commanded that they walk in truth, and whoever remains in the teaching has both the Father and the Son.

Jesus Christ is called the Lord and the Son of the Father, and is a source of grace, mercy, and peace. Deceivers are identified by their refusal to confess that he came in the flesh, and whoever remains in his teaching has both the Father and the Son.

Truth is the basis of the elder's love for the lady and her children, and is known by all who share that love. It remains in them and will be with them forever, and some of the children are found walking in it.

Love is the subject of the commandment the elder urges, that they love one another. It is defined as walking according to God's commandments, and grace, mercy, and peace are with them in truth and love.

The commandment is described as not new but what they have had from the beginning, that they love one another. It is explained that love means walking according to his commandments, and that they should walk in it as they heard from the beginning.

Deceivers are said to have gone out into the world in large numbers, and are those who do not confess that Jesus Christ came in the flesh. They are called the deceiver and the Antichrist, and anyone who welcomes one shares in his evil deeds.

l: teaching of Christ, 2 John, 2 John / Chapter 1
s: The teaching of Christ is the standard by which people are judged: whoever transgresses and does not remain in it does not have God, while whoever remains in it has both the Father and the Son. Anyone who comes without bringing this teaching is not to be received or welcomed.

In 3 John, the elder (John) writes to Gaius, whom he loves, praising him for walking in the truth and for his faithful work toward brothers and strangers. He urges Gaius to send traveling brothers on their way in a manner worthy of God, since they went out for the sake of the Name and took nothing from the Gentiles. He criticizes Diotrephes, who loves to be first, rejects the elder's words, accuses him with wicked words, refuses to receive the brothers, and expels those who would. He commends Demetrius as having a good testimony from all and from the truth itself, and says he hopes to visit Gaius soon to speak face to face.

Writing as the elder, John addresses Gaius with love, prays for his prosperity and health, and says he has no greater joy than hearing his children walk in truth. He says he wrote to the assembly, plans to call attention to Diotrephes's deeds if he comes, vouches for Demetrius, and hopes to see Gaius soon rather than write more with ink and pen.

Gaius is the beloved recipient of the letter, praised because brothers testified to his walking in truth and to his love before the assembly. He is told he does a faithful work for brothers and strangers, is urged to send them forward worthily and to imitate good rather than evil, and is told John hopes to see him soon.

Diotrephes is described as one who loves to be first among the assembly and does not accept what John and his companions say. He unjustly accuses them with wicked words, refuses to receive the brothers, and forbids and throws out of the assembly those who would; John says he will call attention to these deeds if he comes.
Demetrius is said to have the testimony of all and of the truth itself. John adds that he and his companions also testify for him, and that their testimony is true.

Brothers came and testified about Gaius's truth and love before the assembly. They went out for the sake of the Name, taking nothing from the Gentiles, and John says they ought to be received and sent on their journey worthily; Diotrephes refuses to receive them.

Truth is the standard by which John rejoices in Gaius, who walks in truth, and he has no greater joy than hearing his children walk in it. Receiving the traveling brothers makes believers fellow workers for the truth, and Demetrius has the testimony of the truth itself.

l: hospitality toward traveling brothers, 3 John, 3 John / Chapter 1
s: John commends Gaius for his faithful work and love toward brothers and strangers and urges him to send them forward in a way worthy of God. He says such people ought to be received so that believers may be fellow workers for the truth, in contrast to Diotrephes, who refuses them and expels those who welcome them.

Chapter 1 opens the Revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave him to show his servants and which was made known through his angel to John. John greets the seven assemblies in Asia with grace and peace from God, the seven Spirits, and Jesus Christ, and declares that Christ is coming with the clouds. On the isle of Patmos, John is in the Spirit on the Lord's day and hears a voice telling him to write what he sees and send it to seven named assemblies. He sees one like a son of man among seven golden lamp stands, holding seven stars, and falls at his feet as though dead. The figure says he is the first and the last, the Living one who was dead and is alive forever, holds the keys of Death and Hades, and explains that the seven stars are the angels of the seven assemblies and the lamp stands are the assemblies.

Jesus Christ is the one whose Revelation God gave, and he is called the faithful witness, the firstborn of the dead, and the ruler of the kings of the earth. He loves and washed his people from their sins by his blood and made them a Kingdom and priests, and he is said to be coming with the clouds so that every eye will see him. John sees him as one like a son of man among the lamp stands, who identifies himself as the first and the last, the Living one who was dead and is alive forever, holding the keys of Death and Hades.

God gave the Revelation to Jesus Christ to show to his servants what must happen soon. He is described as the one who is and who was and who is to come, and the Lord God calls himself the Alpha and the Omega, the Almighty. Grace and peace are sent from him, and Jesus Christ made believers priests to his God and Father.

John is the servant to whom the Revelation was made known by Christ's angel, and he testified to God's word and the testimony of Jesus Christ about all that he saw. He writes to the seven assemblies as their brother and partner in the oppression, Kingdom, and perseverance in Christ, and was on the isle of Patmos because of God's Word. In the Spirit on the Lord's day he hears a voice and sees the vision of the one like a son of man, falls as dead, is comforted, and is told to write what he has seen, what is, and what will happen hereafter.

The seven assemblies in Asia are the recipients of John's greeting and of the book he is told to write. They are named as Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea. The mystery is explained: the seven lamp stands are the seven assemblies, and the seven stars in Christ's right hand are their angels.

The Revelation is given by God to Jesus Christ, to show his servants the things which must happen soon, and it is made known through his angel to John. A blessing is pronounced on whoever reads, hears, and keeps the words of this prophecy, for the time is near. John is commanded to write it in a book and send it to the seven assemblies, covering what he has seen, what is, and what will happen hereafter.

Chapter 2 contains four letters addressed to the angels of the assemblies in Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, and Thyatira. The speaker, who describes himself with different titles in each letter, says he knows each assembly's works, praising their perseverance, endurance, love, and faith while rebuking specific failings. Ephesus left its first love, Pergamum tolerates the teaching of Balaam and the Nicolaitans, and Thyatira tolerates Jezebel, who seduces his servants into sexual immorality and eating idol sacrifices. Smyrna is told not to fear coming suffering and to be faithful to death. Each letter ends with a call to hear what the Spirit says and a promise to those who overcome.

He speaks each letter under a different description: the one who holds the seven stars and walks among the lamp stands, the first and last who was dead and came to life, the one with the sharp two-edged sword, and the Son of God with eyes like fire and feet like burnished brass. He claims to know each assembly's works, to search minds and hearts, and to give to each according to deeds. He threatens to come swiftly, to make war with the sword of his mouth, and to judge Jezebel and her followers, and he promises rewards to those who overcome.

It is commended for its works, toil, perseverance, intolerance of evil men, testing of false apostles, and hatred of the works of the Nicolaitans. It is rebuked for leaving its first love and told to remember, repent, and do the first works, or its lamp stand will be moved out of its place.

It is known for oppression and poverty, though it is called rich, and it suffers blasphemy from those who claim to be Jews but are a synagogue of Satan. It is told not to fear, since the devil will throw some into prison for testing and oppression for ten days. It is urged to be faithful to death in order to receive the crown of life, and no rebuke is given.

It dwells where Satan's throne is, holds firmly to the speaker's name, and did not deny the faith in the days of Antipas, his faithful witness who was killed among them. It is rebuked because some hold the teaching of Balaam and of the Nicolaitans, and it is told to repent or he will come quickly and war against them with the sword of his mouth.

It is commended for love, faith, service, and patient endurance, with its last works exceeding its first. It is rebuked for tolerating Jezebel. The rest who do not hold her teaching are given no other burden and told to hold firmly to what they have until he comes.

She is a woman in Thyatira who calls herself a prophetess and teaches and seduces the speaker's servants to commit sexual immorality and eat things sacrificed to idols. She was given time to repent but refuses. He will throw her and those who commit adultery with her into a bed of great oppression unless they repent, and will kill her children with Death.

l: the one who overcomes, Revelation, Chapter 2
s: Those who overcome receive promises in each letter: to eat from the tree of life in the Paradise of God, to be unharmed by the second death, and to receive hidden manna and a white stone with a new name. In the last letter, the one who overcomes and keeps his works to the end is given authority over the nations to rule them with a rod of iron, and the morning star.

l: sexual immorality and eating idol sacrifices, Revelation, Chapter 2
s: These practices are condemned as the fruit of false teaching: Balaam taught Balak to put a stumbling block before Israel in this way, and the same teaching is held by some in Pergamum. In Thyatira, Jezebel leads the speaker's servants into them, and she refuses to repent of her sexual immorality.

In Revelation 3, the speaker, who has the seven Spirits of God and the seven stars, dictates messages to the angels of three assemblies: Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea. Sardis is told it has a reputation for being alive but is dead, and is urged to wake up, remember, keep what it received, and repent, though a few there have not defiled their garments. Philadelphia is praised for keeping his word and not denying his name, is given an open door, and is promised protection from the hour of testing. Laodicea is rebuked as lukewarm, self-satisfied, and in fact wretched, poor, blind, and naked, and is counseled to buy gold, white garments, and eye salve, and to repent. Each message closes with a promise to the one who overcomes and a call to hear what the Spirit says to the assemblies.

He addresses Sardis as the one who has the seven Spirits of God and the seven stars, then to Philadelphia as holy and true, holding the key of David, and to Laodicea as the Amen, the Faithful and True Witness, the Beginning of God's creation. He says he knows each assembly's works, rebukes Sardis and Laodicea, praises Philadelphia, and says he is coming quickly. He stands at the door and knocks, promising to dine with whoever opens, and promises overcomers a seat on his throne as he overcame and sat with his Father on his throne.

l: angel of the assembly in Sardis, Revelation, Chapter 3
s: The angel of the assembly in Sardis is the addressee of the first message in this unit, which is written to him. The speaker's words to the assembly come through this angel.

The assembly in Sardis has a reputation of being alive but is dead, and none of its works are found perfected before God. It is told to wake up, strengthen what remains, remember what it received and heard, keep it, and repent, or the speaker will come as a thief. A few names in Sardis did not defile their garments and will walk with him in white.

l: angel of the assembly in Philadelphia, Revelation, Chapter 3
s: The angel of the assembly in Philadelphia is the addressee of the second message in this unit, which is written to him. The speaker's words to the assembly come through this angel.

The assembly in Philadelphia has a little power, kept the speaker's word, and did not deny his name, so he sets before it an open door no one can shut. He will make some of the synagogue of Satan, who say they are Jews but lie, come and worship before its feet and know he loved it. Because it kept his command to endure, he will keep it from the hour of testing, and it is told to hold firmly what it has so no one takes its crown.

l: angel of the assembly in Laodicea, Revelation, Chapter 3
s: The angel of the assembly in Laodicea is the addressee of the third message in this unit, which is written to him. The speaker's words to the assembly come through this angel.

The assembly in Laodicea is neither cold nor hot but lukewarm, so the speaker says he will vomit it out of his mouth. It claims to be rich and in need of nothing, but is wretched, miserable, poor, blind, and naked. It is counseled to buy refined gold, white garments, and eye salve from him, and to be zealous and repent, since he reproves and chastens those he loves.

God is called the speaker's God and also his Father, before whom the speaker will confess the names of overcomers. No works of Sardis are found perfected before him. The overcomer in Philadelphia will be made a pillar in God's temple and have God's name and the name of God's city, the new Jerusalem, written on him.

l: the one who overcomes, Revelation, Chapter 3
s: The one who overcomes is promised, in each message, a reward from the speaker. In Sardis he will be arrayed in white and his name will not be blotted out of the book of life. In Philadelphia he will become a pillar in the temple of God, never leaving it, and receive the names of God, the new Jerusalem, and the speaker. In Laodicea he will sit with the speaker on his throne.

l: Laodicea's lukewarmness and self-sufficiency, Revelation, Chapter 3
s: Laodicea's works are neither cold nor hot, and the speaker says he wishes it were one or the other, because its lukewarmness leads him to vomit it out. It says it is rich and needs nothing, but does not know it is wretched, miserable, poor, blind, and naked. The speaker counsels it to buy gold, white garments, and eye salve and to repent.

The narrator sees a door opened in heaven and hears a trumpet-like voice calling him to come up and be shown what must happen after this. Immediately in the Spirit, he sees a throne in heaven with one sitting on it, who looks like jasper and sardius, with an emerald-like rainbow around it. Around the throne sit twenty-four elders in white garments with gold crowns, and lightnings, sounds, thunders, seven lamps of fire, and a sea of glass like crystal are described. Four living creatures full of eyes, resembling a lion, a calf, a man, and a flying eagle, ceaselessly proclaim God's holiness. When they give glory, the twenty-four elders fall down, worship the one who lives forever, throw their crowns before the throne, and declare him worthy as creator of all things.

God is the one sitting on the throne, whose appearance is like a jasper stone and a sardius. He is called the Lord God, the Almighty, who was, is, and is to come, and who lives forever and ever. He is declared worthy to receive glory, honor, and power because he created all things, which existed and were created by his desire.

The narrator looks and sees a door opened in heaven, and hears a voice like a trumpet telling him to come up to be shown what must happen after this. Immediately he is in the Spirit, and he describes the throne, the elders, and the living creatures he sees.

The throne is set in heaven with one sitting on it, surrounded by a rainbow like an emerald. Lightnings, sounds, and thunders proceed from it, and seven lamps of fire, the seven Spirits of God, burn before it. Before it is a sea of glass like crystal, and the four living creatures are in the middle of it and around it. Twenty-four other thrones surround it, and the elders throw their crowns before it.

The twenty-four elders sit on twenty-four thrones around God's throne, dressed in white garments with gold crowns on their heads. When the living creatures give glory to him who sits on the throne, the elders fall down, worship him, and throw their crowns before the throne. They declare that God is worthy to receive glory, honor, and power because he created all things.

The four living creatures are in the middle of and around the throne, full of eyes before, behind, around, and within, each with six wings. The first is like a lion, the second like a calf, the third has a face like a man, and the fourth is like a flying eagle. They have no rest day and night, saying "Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God, the Almighty," and they give glory, honor, and thanks to the one on the throne.

Heaven has a door that is opened, through which a voice calls the narrator to come up. It contains the throne with the one sitting on it, the twenty-four thrones and elders, the seven lamps of fire, the sea of glass, and the four living creatures.

The four living creatures ceaselessly proclaim God's holiness and give him glory, honor, and thanks. In response, the twenty-four elders fall down before him, worship him who lives forever and ever, and throw their crowns before the throne. They declare him worthy to receive glory, honor, and power as creator of all things.

The narrator sees a book sealed with seven seals in the right hand of him who sat on the throne, and a mighty angel asks who is worthy to open it. No one in heaven, on earth, or under the earth can, and the narrator weeps until one of the elders tells him the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has overcome. The narrator then sees a Lamb standing as though slain, with seven horns and seven eyes, who takes the book from the one on the throne. The four living creatures and twenty-four elders fall before the Lamb and sing a new song praising him for buying people from every tribe, language, people, and nation with his blood and making them kings and priests. Many angels and then every created thing join in praise of the one on the throne and the Lamb, and the living creatures say "Amen" while the elders fall down and worship.

He holds in his right hand a book written inside and outside and sealed with seven seals. The Lamb takes the book from his right hand. He is praised together with the Lamb by every created thing, who give blessing, honor, glory, and dominion to him forever.

l: book (held by him who sat on the throne), Revelation, Chapter 5
s: The book is written inside and outside and sealed shut with seven seals, and it is held in the right hand of him who sat on the throne. No one in heaven, on earth, or under the earth is found able to open it or look in it, until the Lamb takes it from the right hand of the one on the throne.

l: seven seals (of the book), Revelation, Chapter 5
s: The seven seals keep the book sealed shut. A mighty angel asks who is worthy to break them, and no one is found able until the one described as the Lion, who has overcome, is said to open the book and its seven seals. The Lamb is then praised as worthy to open them.

The narrator sees the sealed book, the mighty angel's proclamation, the Lamb, and the worship around the throne, and he hears the voices of the angels and of every created thing. He weeps much because no one is found worthy to open the book, until one of the elders tells him not to weep.

The Lamb is seen standing in the middle of the throne, the four living creatures, and the elders, as though slain, with seven horns and seven eyes, which are the seven Spirits of God sent out into all the earth. He takes the book from the right hand of him who sat on the throne. He is declared worthy to take the book and open its seals because he was killed and bought people for God with his blood, and he receives power, wealth, wisdom, strength, honor, glory, and blessing, and worship from the elders, creatures, angels, and all created things.

One elder tells the narrator not to weep because the Lion of Judah, the Root of David, has overcome. After the Lamb takes the book, the elders fall down before him, each holding a harp and golden bowls of incense, which are the prayers of the saints, and they sing a new song. At the end they fall down and worship.

The four living creatures are around the throne, with the Lamb standing in their midst. They fall down before the Lamb with the elders, each having a harp and golden bowls of incense, and they sing the new song. They say "Amen" to the praise offered by every created thing.

l: redeemed people (bought by the Lamb), Revelation, Chapter 5
s: They are said to have been bought for God with the Lamb's blood out of every tribe, language, people, and nation. They have been made kings and priests to God and will reign on the earth.

The narrator hears the voice of many angels around the throne, the living creatures, and the elders, numbering ten thousands of ten thousands and thousands of thousands. They say with a loud voice that the Lamb who has been killed is worthy to receive power, wealth, wisdom, strength, honor, glory, and blessing. Earlier, a mighty angel proclaims the question of who is worthy to open the book.

Every created thing in heaven, on the earth, under the earth, and on the sea, and everything in them, is heard speaking. They offer blessing, honor, glory, and dominion forever to him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb.

l: worship of the Lamb, Revelation, Chapter 5
s: Worship of the Lamb begins when the living creatures and elders fall down before him with harps and bowls of incense and sing a new song. It widens to include many angels and then every created thing, who join in ascribing blessing, honor, glory, and dominion to the one on the throne and the Lamb. It closes with the creatures' "Amen" and the elders falling down and worshiping.

In Chapter 6 the Lamb opens the first six of the seven seals, and each of the first four living creatures calls out "Come" as a differently colored horse appears. The white horse's rider has a bow and a crown and goes out conquering. The red horse's rider is given power to take peace from the earth and a great sword. The black horse's rider holds a balance, and a voice announces the price of wheat and barley. The pale horse's rider is named Death, followed by Hades, and is given authority over a fourth of the earth. At the fifth seal the souls of those killed for the Word of God cry out under the altar and are given white robes and told to rest a while longer. At the sixth seal a great earthquake and cosmic upheaval occur, and all classes of people hide in caves and rocks, asking the mountains to fall on them because the great day of wrath of the one on the throne and the Lamb has come.

The Lamb opens the first six of the seven seals in turn, each opening prompting a living creature's call or a major event. His wrath, together with that of the one on the throne, is what the people of the earth try to hide from.

l: seven seals (of the book), Revelation, Chapter 6
s: Six of the seven seals are opened by the Lamb in this chapter. The first four release horses and riders, the fifth reveals the souls of the slain under the altar, and the sixth brings an earthquake and cosmic signs.

l: rider on the white horse, Revelation, Chapter 6
s: He holds a bow and is given a crown. He goes out conquering and to conquer.

l: rider on the red horse, Revelation, Chapter 6
s: He is given power to take peace from the earth so that people kill one another. He is also given a great sword.

l: rider on the black horse, Revelation, Chapter 6
s: He holds a balance in his hand. A voice from the middle of the four living creatures announces a choenix of wheat for a denarius and three choenix of barley for a denarius, and says not to damage the oil and the wine.

Death is the name of the rider on the pale horse, and Hades follows with him. He is given authority over one fourth of the earth to kill with the sword, famine, death, and the wild animals of the earth.

l: souls of the slain, Revelation, Chapter 6
s: They are seen underneath the altar, having been killed for the Word of God and the testimony of the Lamb. They cry out asking how long until the Master judges and avenges their blood, and each is given a white robe and told to rest a while until their fellow servants and brothers who will also be killed complete their course.

l: great earthquake and cosmic signs, Revelation, Chapter 6
s: At the sixth seal a great earthquake occurs, the sun turns black as sackcloth and the moon becomes as blood. The stars fall to the earth, the sky is removed like a rolled-up scroll, and every mountain and island is moved from its place.

l: kings and people of the earth, Revelation, Chapter 6
s: The kings, princes, commanding officers, the rich, the strong, and every slave and free person hide in caves and among mountain rocks. They call on the mountains and rocks to fall on them and hide them from the face of the one on the throne and the wrath of the Lamb.

l: great day of his wrath, Revelation, Chapter 6
s: The people of the earth declare that the great day of his wrath has come. They ask who is able to stand.

The narrator sees four angels at the four corners of the earth holding back the four winds so that no harm comes to earth, sea, or trees. Another angel rising from the sunrise, holding the seal of the living God, commands them to wait until the bondservants of God are sealed on their foreheads. The narrator hears the number sealed, 144,000, with 12,000 from each of twelve tribes of the children of Israel. He then sees an uncountable multitude from every nation, tribe, people, and language standing before the throne and the Lamb in white robes with palm branches, crying out salvation to God and the Lamb, while the angels, elders, and four living creatures worship. One of the elders explains that the multitude came out of the great suffering, washed their robes in the Lamb's blood, and now serve God in his temple, where he shelters them, the Lamb shepherds them, and God wipes away every tear.

The four angels stand at the four corners of the earth holding the four winds so that no wind blows on the earth, sea, or any tree. They are the ones to whom it was given to harm the earth and the sea, and they are told to hold off until the bondservants of God are sealed.

Another angel ascends from the sunrise carrying the seal of the living God. He cries out loudly to the four angels not to harm the earth, the sea, or the trees until the bondservants of God have been sealed on their foreheads.

God is called the living God, whose seal is carried by the angel from the sunrise, and the sealed people are his bondservants. He sits on the throne and receives the worship of the multitude and the angels, who ascribe blessing, glory, wisdom, thanksgiving, honor, power, and might to him forever. He will spread his tabernacle over the multitude and wipe away every tear from their eyes.

The Lamb is praised alongside God by the great multitude, who cry that salvation belongs to God and to the Lamb. His blood is where the multitude washed their robes white, and he stands in the middle of the throne, shepherding them and leading them to springs of life-giving waters.

l: one hundred forty-four thousand, Revelation, Chapter 7
s: The bondservants of God are sealed on their foreheads, and their number is heard to be 144,000. They are sealed out of every tribe of the children of Israel, 12,000 from each of twelve tribes.

The children of Israel are the people from whose tribes the 144,000 are sealed. The tribes named are Judah, Reuben, Gad, Asher, Naphtali, Manasseh, Simeon, Levi, Issachar, Zebulun, Joseph, and Benjamin, each with 12,000 sealed.

The great multitude is a crowd no one could count, from every nation, tribe, people, and language, standing before the throne and the Lamb in white robes with palm branches. They cry out that salvation belongs to God and the Lamb. The elder explains that they came out of the great suffering and washed their robes in the Lamb's blood. They serve God day and night in his temple and will never again hunger, thirst, or be scorched by the sun or heat.

l: elder (who spoke to John), Revelation, Chapter 7
s: One of the elders asks the narrator who the people in white robes are and where they came from. When the narrator defers to him, the elder explains that they came out of the great suffering and washed their robes in the Lamb's blood, then describes their service and care in God's presence.

The narrator sees the four angels, the angel from the sunrise, the great multitude, and the worship around the throne, and he hears the number of the sealed. When the elder asks who the robed multitude are, he answers "My lord, you know," and receives the explanation from the elder.

When the seventh seal is opened, heaven falls silent for about half an hour, and seven angels standing before God are given seven trumpets. Another angel with a golden censer adds incense to the saints' prayers at the altar, then fills the censer with altar fire and throws it to the earth, causing thunders, sounds, lightnings, and an earthquake. The seven angels prepare to sound, and the first four trumpets bring destruction in turn: hail and fire mixed with blood burn a third of the earth and trees, a burning mountain turns a third of the sea to blood, the star Wormwood embitters a third of the waters, and a third of the sun, moon, and stars is darkened. An eagle flying in mid heaven cries out a threefold woe on those who dwell on the earth because of the three trumpets still to come.
The seven angels stand before God and are given seven trumpets. They prepare to sound, and four of them sound in this unit, each bringing a calamity, while three remain yet to sound.

Seven trumpets are given to the seven angels who stand before God. Four are sounded in this unit, each followed by a destructive event affecting a third of the earth, sea, waters, or heavenly lights, and three are still to come.

l: angel with the golden censer, Revelation, Chapter 8
s: Another angel stands over the altar with a golden censer and is given much incense to add to the prayers of all the saints. The smoke goes up before God from his hand, after which he fills the censer with altar fire and throws it on the earth, followed by thunders, sounds, lightnings, and an earthquake.

The earth receives the fire thrown from the censer, followed by thunders, sounds, lightnings, and an earthquake. At the first trumpet, one third of the earth is burned up, along with one third of the trees and all green grass. The eagle announces woe to those who dwell on it.
When the first angel sounds, hail and fire mixed with blood are thrown to the earth. One third of the earth is burned up, one third of the trees are burned up, and all green grass is burned up.

At the second trumpet, something like a great burning mountain is thrown into the sea. One third of the sea becomes blood, one third of the living creatures in it die, and one third of the ships are destroyed.

Wormwood is the name of a great star that falls from the sky burning like a torch at the third trumpet. It falls on one third of the rivers and on the springs of water, making one third of the waters bitter as wormwood, and many people die from them.

An eagle is seen and heard flying in mid heaven after the fourth trumpet. It cries with a loud voice a threefold woe to those who dwell on the earth because of the blasts of the three trumpets yet to sound.

In Chapter 9, the fifth angel sounds and a star fallen from the sky is given the key to the pit of the abyss; he opens it and smoke darkens the sun and air. Locusts with scorpion-like power come out and torment, but do not kill, people without God's seal for five months, and their king is the angel of the abyss, named Abaddon in Hebrew and Apollyon in Greek. After the first woe passes, the sixth angel sounds and a voice from the golden altar orders him to free the four angels bound at the Euphrates. Those angels are freed to kill one third of mankind, and an army of two hundred million horsemen with lion-headed horses kills them by fire, smoke, and sulfur. The rest of mankind does not repent of their idolatry, murders, sorceries, sexual immorality, or thefts.
The fifth angel sounds his trumpet, which begins the first woe. After he sounds, a star fallen from the sky is seen receiving the key to the abyss.

l: star (fallen from the sky, fifth angel), Revelation, Chapter 9
s: The narrator sees a star that had fallen from the sky to the earth after the fifth angel sounded. The key to the pit of the abyss is given to him, and he opens the pit.

l: pit of the abyss, Revelation, Chapter 9
s: The pit is opened with the key given to the fallen star, and smoke like that of a burning furnace rises from it, darkening the sun and the air. Locusts come out of the smoke, and the pit's king is the angel of the abyss.

Locusts come out of the smoke on the earth with power like that of scorpions. They are forbidden to harm the grass, green things, or trees, and may only torment, not kill, people without God's seal for five months. They look like war horses with golden crowns, human faces, women's hair, lions' teeth, iron breastplates, noisy wings like chariots, and scorpion tails with stingers. Their king is the angel of the abyss.

l: people without God's seal, Revelation, Chapter 9
s: People who lack God's seal on their foreheads are the only ones the locusts are allowed to hurt. They are tormented for five months as by a scorpion's sting, so that they seek death but cannot find it, and death flees from them.
Abaddon is the Hebrew name of the angel of the abyss, who is king over the locusts. His Greek name is Apollyon.
The sixth angel sounds his trumpet after the first woe has passed. A voice from the horns of the golden altar before God tells him to free the four angels bound at the Euphrates.

The four angels are bound at the great river Euphrates until the sixth angel is told to free them. When freed, they, having been prepared for that hour, day, month, and year, are to kill one third of mankind.

One third of mankind is killed by the fire, smoke, and sulfur from the horses' mouths. The rest, who survive these plagues, do not repent of worshiping demons and idols, nor of their murders, sorceries, sexual immorality, or thefts.

The armies of horsemen number two hundred million, a number the narrator heard. Their riders wear breastplates of fiery red, hyacinth blue, and sulfur yellow, and their horses have lions' heads. Fire, smoke, and sulfur come from the horses' mouths, and their serpent-like tails with heads also harm.
The three plagues are the fire, the smoke, and the sulfur that proceed out of the horses' mouths. By them one third of mankind is killed.

The narrator sees a mighty angel descend from the sky, clothed with a cloud, with a rainbow on his head, a face like the sun, and feet like pillars of fire. The angel holds a little open book, stands with one foot on the sea and one on the land, and cries out like a roaring lion, whereupon the seven thunders speak. A voice from the sky forbids the narrator to write what the thunders said. The angel swears by the eternal Creator that there will be no more delay and that the mystery of God will be finished in the days of the seventh angel's sounding. The narrator is told to take the little book, eats it, finds it sweet as honey in his mouth but bitter in his stomach, and is told he must prophesy again over many peoples, nations, languages, and kings.

The mighty angel comes down from the sky clothed with a cloud, with a rainbow on his head, a face like the sun, and feet like pillars of fire. He stands with his right foot on the sea and his left on the land, holding a little open book, and cries out like a roaring lion. He lifts his right hand and swears by the eternal Creator that there will be no more delay and that the mystery of God will be finished in the days of the seventh angel's sounding. He then gives the little book to the narrator, telling him to eat it and warning that it will be bitter in his stomach but sweet as honey in his mouth.

The narrator sees the mighty angel and is about to write what the seven thunders said, but a voice from the sky forbids it. He is told to take the open book from the angel, asks the angel for it, and eats it, finding it sweet in his mouth and bitter in his stomach. He is then told that he must prophesy again over many peoples, nations, languages, and kings.

l: little book (in the angel's hand), Revelation, Chapter 10
s: The little book is held open in the mighty angel's hand as he stands on the sea and the land. The narrator is told to take it, and he does and eats it. It is as sweet as honey in his mouth, but it makes his stomach bitter.

The seven thunders utter their voices when the angel cries out with a loud voice like a lion's roar. The narrator is about to write what they said, but a voice from the sky commands him to seal up their words and not write them, so their content remains undisclosed.

God is described by the angel's oath as the one who lives forever and ever and who created heaven, the earth, and the sea and everything in them. He is said to have declared the mystery of God to his servants the prophets.
The angel swears that the mystery of God will be finished in the days of the seventh angel's voice, when he is about to sound. It is said that God declared this mystery to his servants the prophets.

The narrator is given a reed and told to measure God's temple, the altar, and its worshipers, while leaving out the outer court, which has been given to the nations, who will trample the holy city for forty-two months. God's two witnesses prophesy for 1,260 days in sackcloth, wielding fire, power over rain, water, and plagues, until the beast from the abyss kills them. Their bodies lie in the great city, where those who dwell on the earth celebrate for three and a half days, until God's breath enters the witnesses, they stand, and they ascend to heaven in a cloud. A great earthquake then strikes the city, killing seven thousand, and the survivors give glory to God. The seventh angel sounds, voices and the twenty-four elders proclaim that the kingdom of the world has become the Kingdom of the Lord and his Christ, and God's temple in heaven opens, revealing the ark of the covenant amid lightning, thunder, an earthquake, and hail.

The two witnesses are given power to prophesy for 1,260 days clothed in sackcloth, and are called the two olive trees and two lamp stands standing before the Lord of the earth. They devour enemies with fire, shut the sky, turn waters to blood, and strike the earth with plagues, until the beast kills them. After three and a half days God's breath enters them, they stand, and they are called up to heaven in a cloud as their enemies watch.

God gives power to his two witnesses and breathes life into them after three and a half days, then calls them up to heaven. He is worshiped by the twenty-four elders as Lord God, the Almighty, who has taken his great power and reigned, and the survivors of the earthquake give glory to him as the God of heaven.

Christ is referred to as the Lord of the two witnesses, who was crucified in the great city. Voices in heaven declare that the kingdom of the world has become the Kingdom of the Lord and of his Christ, and that he will reign forever and ever.

l: temple of the tabernacle of the testimony, Revelation, Chapter 11
s: The narrator is told to measure God's temple, the altar, and those who worship in it. The court outside the temple is to be left unmeasured because it has been given to the nations.
The holy city will be trodden under foot by the nations for forty-two months.

The great city, spiritually called Sodom and Egypt and the place where the Lord was crucified, is where the witnesses' dead bodies lie in the street. A great earthquake there makes a tenth of it fall and kills seven thousand people.

l: beast from the abyss, Revelation, Chapter 11
s: The beast that comes up out of the abyss makes war on the two witnesses once they finish their testimony. It overcomes and kills them.

l: those who dwell on the earth, Revelation, Chapter 11
s: Those who dwell on the earth rejoice and are glad over the dead witnesses, giving gifts to one another because the two prophets had tormented them. People from the peoples, tribes, languages, and nations look at the bodies for three and a half days and refuse to let them be buried.

The twenty-four elders, seated on their thrones before God's throne, fall on their faces and worship God. They give thanks that he has taken his great power and reigned, and speak of the nations' anger, his wrath, the judgment of the dead, and the reward for his servants.
A great earthquake occurs on the day the witnesses ascend, causing a tenth of the city to fall and killing seven thousand people. The rest are terrified and give glory to the God of heaven.
God's temple in heaven is opened and the ark of the Lord's covenant is seen inside it. Lightnings, sounds, thunders, an earthquake, and great hail follow.

l: kingdom of the world, Revelation, Chapter 11
s: After the seventh angel sounds, loud voices in heaven declare that the kingdom of the world has become the Kingdom of the Lord and of his Christ. He will reign forever and ever.

Chapter 12 describes a woman clothed with the sun, who is with child and crowned with twelve stars, and a great red dragon with seven heads and ten horns who waits to devour her child. The child is born and caught up to God and his throne, while the woman flees to a place God has prepared in the wilderness. War breaks out in heaven, where Michael and his angels defeat the dragon, the old serpent called the devil and Satan, and he and his angels are thrown down to the earth. A loud voice in heaven proclaims salvation and the Kingdom of God, saying the brothers overcame the accuser by the Lamb's blood and their testimony, and warns the earth of the devil's wrath. The enraged dragon persecutes the woman, who is given eagle's wings and helped by the earth against his river, so he goes off to make war on the rest of her offspring.

l: woman clothed with the sun, Revelation, Chapter 12
s: She appears as a great sign in heaven, clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet and a crown of twelve stars, and cries out in labor. After she bears a son, she flees to a place God prepared in the wilderness, where she is nourished for 1,260 days, a time, times, and half a time. She is given two wings of the great eagle and is helped by the earth, which swallows the river the serpent spews after her.

A great red dragon with seven heads, ten horns, and seven crowns, he draws a third of the stars to the earth with his tail and stands ready to devour the woman's child. He is identified as the old serpent, the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world, and is defeated in war and thrown down to earth with his angels. Furious and knowing his time is short, he persecutes the woman, spews a river after her, and then goes to make war on the rest of her offspring.

l: male child (the woman's son), Revelation, Chapter 12
s: The woman gives birth to a son, a male child who is to rule all the nations with a rod of iron. He is caught up to God and to his throne, escaping the dragon who wanted to devour him.
Michael and his angels make war on the dragon and his angels in the sky. They prevail, and the dragon and his angels are thrown out of heaven.

God has prepared a place in the wilderness where the woman is nourished, and the woman's child is caught up to him and to his throne. A loud voice in heaven proclaims that his salvation, power, and Kingdom have come, along with the authority of his Christ. His commandments are kept by the rest of the woman's offspring.

The voice in heaven calls them the brothers whom the accuser accuses before God day and night. They overcame him by the Lamb's blood and the word of their testimony, not loving their life even to death.

l: rest of the woman's offspring, Revelation, Chapter 12
s: They are described as those who keep God's commandments and hold Jesus' testimony. The dragon, angry with the woman, goes away to make war on them.

Heaven is the setting of the signs of the woman and the dragon and of the war in which the dragon and his angels lose their place. A loud voice there proclaims God's salvation and Kingdom, and the heavens and their inhabitants are told to rejoice because the accuser has been thrown down.

The dragon draws a third of the stars to the earth, and later he and his angels are thrown down onto it. The earth and the sea are warned of woe because the devil has come down in great wrath. The earth helps the woman by opening its mouth and swallowing the river the dragon spewed.

Michael and his angels fight the dragon and his angels in the sky. The dragon's side does not prevail and no place is found for them in heaven, so the dragon, the old serpent, and his angels are thrown down to the earth.

The narrator sees a first beast rise out of the sea with ten horns, seven heads, and blasphemous names. The dragon gives it power, a throne, and great authority. Its fatal head wound is healed, the earth marvels and worships both the dragon and the beast, and the beast is permitted to blaspheme God, make war on the saints for forty-two months, and overcome them. A second beast rises out of the earth, speaks like a dragon, exercises the first beast's authority, performs signs including fire from the sky, and deceives those who dwell on the earth into making an image of the first beast. The second beast gives the image breath so it speaks and has those who refuse to worship it killed, forces all people to receive a mark on the right hand or forehead without which none may buy or sell, and the chapter closes by identifying the beast's number as 666, the number of a man.

The first beast rises out of the sea with ten horns and seven heads, ten crowns on its horns and blasphemous names on its heads, and looks like a leopard with bear's feet and a lion's mouth. The dragon gives it power, throne, and authority, and its fatally wounded head is healed. It is worshiped, speaks great things and blasphemy against God for forty-two months, makes war on the saints and overcomes them, and receives authority over every tribe, people, language, and nation.

The second beast comes up out of the earth with two horns like a lamb but speaks like a dragon. It exercises all the first beast's authority in its presence and makes the earth's inhabitants worship the first beast. It performs great signs, including bringing fire down from the sky, and deceives people into making an image of the first beast. It gives breath to the image and imposes the mark on all people.
The dragon gives the first beast its power, throne, and great authority. People worship the dragon because he gave his authority to the beast. The second beast speaks like a dragon.

l: image of the beast, Revelation, Chapter 13
s: The image is made at the urging of the second beast, who tells those on the earth to make it for the first beast that had the sword wound and lived. The second beast is permitted to give it breath, so that it speaks and causes those who will not worship it to be killed.

l: mark of the beast, Revelation, Chapter 13
s: The second beast causes all people, small and great, rich and poor, free and slave, to be given a mark on their right hands or foreheads. No one can buy or sell without it. The mark is the name of the beast or the number of his name.
The number 666 is given as the number of the beast and is said to be the number of a man. The text calls for wisdom and understanding from anyone who would calculate it.

l: saints and martyrs of Jesus, Revelation, Chapter 13
s: The saints are made war upon by the first beast, who is permitted to overcome them. The text says that captivity and death by the sword are to come to those appointed for them, and calls this the endurance and the faith of the saints.
